title: Nolan Is Coming to Mumbai. 'The Odyssey' Just Made India a First-Stop on the Map — and Locked Every IMAX Screen in the Country.
excerpt: Christopher Nolan, Matt Damon and Tom Holland will walk an Indian red carpet for the first time. The price of admission? Spider-Man doesn't get IMAX, and half of Bollywood blinked.
body:
It takes a particular kind of pull to make a country rearrange its summer around you. **Christopher Nolan** has it. The most worshipped working director in India — the man whose name sells out 70mm shows months in advance, whose *Oppenheimer* and *Interstellar* and *Dunkirk* are spoken about in Mumbai multiplexes the way scripture is quoted — is finally coming to the country that has adored him from afar. And he isn't coming quietly.

<youtube></youtube>

**The Odyssey**, Nolan's $250-million adaptation of Homer's epic, will hold its first-ever official Indian premiere in Mumbai this July, ahead of the worldwide release on **July 17, 2026**. Universal Pictures has slotted Mumbai onto the global tour beside London, Paris and New York — and for a Nolan film, that placement is not a courtesy. It is a statement about where the audience actually lives now.

He is not arriving alone. **Matt Damon**, who plays Odysseus, the war-weary king of Ithaca, and **Tom Holland**, cast as his son Telemachus, will be on the carpet. So will Academy Award-winning producer **Emma Thomas**, Nolan's wife and lifelong collaborator. The venue is the giveaway: the PVR Icon IMAX at Phoenix Palladium, the kind of screen Nolan treats as a cathedral. This is a man who shot the entire film on brand-new IMAX 70mm film cameras — the first feature ever made that way — so of course he wants the Indian unveiling to happen on the format that justifies the obsession.

> The first time a Nolan-directed film will have an official premiere in India — a landmark moment for Hollywood-India cinematic engagement.

And here is where it gets deliciously ruthless. Because *The Odyssey* was shot end-to-end in IMAX, the format is its birthright, and Nolan's long partnership with the brand means every IMAX screen in India — and globally — plays his film exclusively for a minimum of three weeks. The casualty? **Spider-Man: Brand New Day**, arriving just thirteen days later on July 30, will skip IMAX in India entirely for the first time in the wall-crawler's modern run. Sony is steering audiences toward PXL, 4DX, ScreenX and Dolby instead. Tom Holland is, somehow, in both films — premiering one on the very screens that just shut the other out. You couldn't script the irony.

Bollywood read the room and stepped back. **Ajay Devgn's** *Dhamaal 4*, once parked on July 17, slid a full week earlier to July 10 rather than stand in the path of the Greek tide. Exhibitors are clearing the runway. When a Nolan film lands, the calendar bends around it — and in 2026, the calendar bent in Mumbai.

The cast Nolan assembled reads like a fever dream: alongside Damon and Holland, there's **Anne Hathaway**, **Zendaya**, **Robert Pattinson**, **Lupita Nyong'o** and **Charlize Theron** sailing through Homer's wine-dark sea. Filmed across multiple countries, it is reportedly the most expensive and most physically ambitious production of Nolan's career — all practical scale, real locations, real water, no green-screen shortcuts. The kind of cinema that practically demands the biggest screen you can find.

For the diaspora, the timing is a gift. Nolan's catalogue is being quietly repositioned for the moment: *Interstellar* lands on Hulu and *The Prestige* on Peacock on July 1, perfect for a pre-*Odyssey* rewatch from a couch in New Jersey or a flat in Wembley. The Odyssey opens worldwide on July 17 — same day across the US, UK, Canada and India — so NRIs won't be waiting on a delayed release for once. IMAX 70mm engagements are already being mapped in the major North American and UK markets, and given the three-week lockout, booking early isn't paranoia, it's strategy.

There's something poetic about *this* film being the one to plant Nolan's flag in India. The Odyssey is, at its heart, a story about the long, brutal journey home — about a man crossing the known world to return to where he belongs. Nolan has spent two decades commanding India's biggest screens from thousands of miles away. In July, he finally makes the trip himself. The hero comes home, and so, in a sense, does the filmmaker his Indian audience never stopped waiting for.
